CHAPTER 1 OF 6 · HIP BLOCKS

Anatomy: the lumbar plexus and the hip

Every hip block is a choice of which branch of the lumbar plexus to catch, where. Learn where the nerves cross the groin and which of them supply the joint, and the choice of block follows.

KEY POINTS

The lumbar plexus (L1–L4, with T12) forms inside psoas. The three nerves that matter here: femoral (L2–L4), lateral femoral cutaneous (L2–L3) and obturator (L2–L4).
Femoral and LFCN leave the lateral border of psoas and run on iliacus under fascia iliaca. The obturator leaves the medial border and runs in the pelvis, outside the fascia iliaca compartment.
At the groin the femoral nerve is lateral to the artery and outside the femoral sheath; the LFCN passes under the inguinal ligament near the ASIS.
The anterior hip capsule (most of the joint’s sensory supply) is supplied by the femoral, obturator and accessory obturator nerves; the posterior capsule by the nerve to quadratus femoris, sciatic and superior gluteal branches.
Hip pain is often felt in the knee: the femoral and obturator nerves supply both joints.

Who supplies the hip joint

Hilton’s law: a nerve that supplies a muscle crossing a joint also supplies the joint. So the hip gets branches from the femoral, obturator and sciatic territories, and the pattern varies between people.

Anterior capsule (the main source of pain after fracture and arthroplasty): femoral nerve (high articular branches that leave the nerve above the inguinal ligament; classically also from the nerve to rectus femoris), obturator nerve, and the accessory obturator nerve when present.
Posterior capsule: nerve to quadratus femoris (the main supply), with branches from the sciatic nerve and the superior gluteal nerve (and in some studies the inferior gluteal nerve).
Overlying skin: LFCN laterally; subcostal and iliohypogastric branches over the iliac crest and trochanter; cluneal nerves over the buttock.

Why PENG works (and what it doesn’t do)

KEY POINT

The logic in four lines

The femoral and accessory obturator branches to the anterior capsule cross the bone between the AIIS and the iliopubic eminence, under the psoas tendon.
Local anaesthetic placed on that bone, under the tendon, catches them before they reach the capsule, while the femoral nerve trunk lies more superficially, on iliopsoas under fascia iliaca.
So the joint is numbed and the quadriceps usually works. The skin is not numbed (no cutaneous nerve runs there).
The obturator branches arrive lower and further in, so they are caught inconsistently, and the posterior capsule not at all.

EXAM PEARL

For the viva

“The anterior hip capsule is supplied by the femoral, obturator and accessory obturator nerves; the posterior capsule by the nerve to quadratus femoris, with sciatic and superior gluteal branches. A PENG block puts local anaesthetic under the psoas tendon between the AIIS and the iliopubic eminence, where the femoral and accessory obturator articular branches run, so it treats capsular pain while sparing the quadriceps. It doesn’t cover the skin, so for arthroplasty I add an LFCN block.”

NOTE

Deeper options (for completeness)

The lumbar plexus (psoas) block, including the ultrasound “shamrock” view, blocks the femoral, LFCN and obturator nerves at their origin. It is a deep block with risks of epidural spread, retroperitoneal haematoma and toxicity; it has largely been replaced by the anterior blocks on this page for hip surgery.

CHAPTER 2 OF 6 · HIP · PERICAPSULAR

PENG block (pericapsular nerve group)

Local anaesthetic on bone beneath the psoas tendon, between the anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) and the iliopubic eminence, where the high articular branches of the femoral nerve and the accessory obturator nerve cross the front of the hip capsule. It treats hip joint pain and usually leaves the quadriceps working. It does not numb the skin.

USE IT FOR

Neck of femur fracture (pain, positioning for spinal)
Intertrochanteric fracture (before surgery)
Hemiarthroplasty or THA (+ LFCN for the incision)
When early walking matters
Chronic hip pain (diagnostic block)
POSITION
Supine, hip neutral
PROBE
Linear (curvilinear if deep), along the superior pubic ramus from the AIIS
NEEDLE
80–100 mm echogenic, in-plane, lateral to medial, to bone under the psoas tendon
DOSE
20 ml of 0.2% ropivacaine (40 mg). With an LFCN block: total 25 ml, 50 mg
COVERS
Anterior hip capsule (articular branches). No skin.

Position

Supine, hip in neutral. Stand on the side to be blocked, screen opposite. In a large patient, a pillow under the buttock and tape (or an assistant) to lift the abdominal fold keep the probe on the AIIS-to-eminence line.

Equipment
Linear probe; curvilinear when the target is deeper than about 5 cm
80–100 mm echogenic needle (the target is deep and the path steep)
20 ml of 0.2% ropivacaine (25 ml if adding an LFCN block)
Monitoring, IV access and the local anaesthetic toxicity kit within reach
Landmarks and scanning

Transverse on the ASIS, then slide caudally onto the AIIS. Keep the lateral end there and rotate the medial end caudally about 45°, so the probe lies along the superior pubic ramus, roughly parallel to the inguinal crease. Slide or tilt until AIIS, psoas tendon and iliopubic eminence share one view. The femoral artery should sit at the medial edge of the image, superficial: your safety landmark.

Line to say out loud: ASIS → AIIS → psoas tendon → iliopubic eminence → pubic ramus. Tilting caudally brings the femoral head into view; come back up to the ramus.

Needle approach

In-plane, lateral to medial, entering 1–2 cm lateral to the probe so the shaft clears the AIIS. Through sartorius (or rectus femoris), fascia iliaca and iliopsoas, then under the psoas tendon to bone. Withdraw 1 mm and aspirate.

The skin entry is close to the LFCN: if infiltration or the needle produces a shoot down the lateral thigh, move the entry point.

Sonoanatomy

Labels to know: AIIS, iliopubic eminence, psoas tendon, iliopsoas, femoral artery and nerve, pectineus. The tendon is a bright oval in the groove between the two bony landmarks, under the much larger, darker iliopsoas muscle belly.

Iliopsoas
Target and deposition

The musculofascial plane between the psoas tendon and the periosteum of the ilium, between the AIIS and the eminence. Correct: the tendon lifts off the bone and fluid spreads along the bone medially and laterally. Wrong: a swelling inside iliopsoas (intramuscular, short of bone), or fluid tracking superficially towards the femoral nerve.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

20 ml of 0.2% ropivacaine (40 mg)

With an LFCN block, add 5 ml of 0.2% there: total 25 ml, 50 mg. Give it in 5 ml aliquots with aspiration. Don’t top up beyond the plan because the lift looks small: bigger volumes make femoral nerve spread and quadriceps weakness more likely.

Local anaesthetic toxicity: Keep the total dose within the maximum for the patient’s weight, especially with bilateral blocks or when combining blocks.

Covers: The anterior hip capsule (femoral and accessory obturator articular branches; obturator branches inconsistently). No skin: add an LFCN block or infiltration for the incision.

MECHANISM

The anterior capsule carries most of the joint’s sensory supply. In cadavers, high articular branches of the femoral nerve run between the AIIS and the iliopubic eminence, and the accessory obturator nerve, when present, crosses the eminence. Fluid under the psoas tendon sits right there. The obturator nerve’s articular branches reach the capsule further medially and inferiorly (near the inferomedial acetabulum), so a PENG block reaches them inconsistently.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Good for hip joint pain on movement (positioning, flexion). Imaging in patients shows the injectate staying mostly in and around iliopsoas, so think of it mainly as a block of the femoral (and accessory obturator) articular branches. Motor sparing is likely at about 20 ml, not guaranteed: test quadriceps strength before the patient stands.

WHAT IT MISSES
The skin incision (LFCN laterally; subcostal and iliohypogastric branches over the buttock).
The posterior capsule (nerve to quadratus femoris, sciatic, superior gluteal branches): relevant for a posterior approach.
The femoral shaft and lateral thigh: fixation with a sliding hip screw or nail is less well covered than arthroplasty.
Obturator articular branches: often.
Complications and how to avoid them
Quadriceps weakness from spread to the femoral nerve (volume, or a superficial or intramuscular injection). Warn the patient and the ward: falls risk.
Vascular puncture: femoral artery and vein medially; small vessels near the pubic ramus (for example pubic branches) along the path. Colour Doppler, aspirate, aliquots.
LFCN injury at the skin entry.
Intra-articular or intraneural injection: rare; stop with high pressure or pain.
Local anaesthetic toxicity, especially when adding other blocks.
Practical pearls
Bone, tendon, bone: AIIS laterally, eminence medially, tendon in the groove between.
The tendon must lift off bone. A swelling in the muscle is the wrong plane.
PENG is for the joint, not the skin: add the LFCN for an anterior or lateral incision.
Femoral artery at the medial edge of the screen: you are not going there.
Stiff to inject on bone? The tip may be in periosteum, tendon or capsule (iliofemoral ligament): back 1 mm or turn the bevel.
Test quadriceps before the first walk. Motor sparing is likely, not certain.
Consultant corner
Arthroplasty versus fixation. PENG suits capsular pain: displaced intracapsular fractures, hemiarthroplasty and total hip arthroplasty.
Screw or nail? The pain is the lateral thigh and the femur below the capsule: a supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block (femoral plus LFCN) usually fits better. Before surgery, PENG often still helps an intertrochanteric fracture.
Which incision? Anterior and anterolateral approaches: PENG plus LFCN covers most of it. A posterior approach crosses the buttock (not LFCN territory) and the posterior capsule: add surgical infiltration.
PENG versus supra-inguinal fascia iliaca. In trials the two give similar pain relief (hip fracture before surgery; total hip arthroplasty after it). PENG preserves quadriceps and hip adductor strength better. Choose PENG when early walking matters; choose fascia iliaca when you also want the anterior and lateral thigh numb, or for femoral fractures.
The hard patient. Obese: curvilinear probe, a steeper approach, an assistant to retract the pannus. After previous hip surgery or with heterotopic bone, the bony landmarks still guide you; the tendon may be hard to see.
Volume and the quadriceps. At 20 ml, motor sparing is common, not reliable: in one hip arthroplasty trial about half had some quadriceps weakness at 3 hours and a quarter at 6 hours. Test the quadriceps before standing; don’t exceed the department’s 20 ml.
The cadaver numbers. Dye reached the femoral nerve trunk in half the specimens at 20 ml and in all at 30 ml; the femoral-sparing volume (90% of cases) was about 13 ml.
Anticoagulated or on antiplatelets? PENG is deep, on bone, and not easily compressed. Current ASRA and European (ESAIC/ESRA) guidance treats deep, non-compressible blocks more like neuraxial ones; weigh the benefit (often a single-shot PENG or fascia iliaca is still worth it) against the bleeding risk, and prefer a superficial, compressible block when the drug is fully active.
Catheters under the psoas tendon have been described; they are not standard.
Frontier: what’s new
How does it really work? CT imaging in patients shows PENG injectate staying mostly within the fascia of iliacus and psoas, with little capsular spread and none into the obturator foramen. Cadaver work agrees that the obturator articular branches are rarely reached. The analgesia is probably from the femoral nerve’s articular branches inside iliopsoas: it is a ‘femoral articular’ block more than a true pericapsular one.
PENG plus LFCN versus fascia iliaca. A recent meta-analysis of six hip surgery trials favoured the combination for quadriceps strength and earlier walking, with slightly lower resting pain and no clear difference in opioid use.
PENG versus local infiltration after total hip arthroplasty: similar pain and opioid use in pooled trials. The PROSPECT guideline for total hip arthroplasty recommends fascia iliaca block or local infiltration analgesia (with paracetamol, an NSAID and IV dexamethasone); PENG had too little evidence when it was written.
Chronic hip pain. The same articular branches (between the AIIS and eminence, and at the inferomedial acetabulum) are targets for radiofrequency ablation and cryoneurolysis in patients unfit for arthroplasty.
Exam corner

PRACTICE QUESTION

Describe the sensory innervation of the hip joint. Which part does a PENG block target, and why is it described as motor sparing?

Model answer points
Hilton’s law: the nerves supplying the muscles that cross the hip also supply the joint.
Anterior capsule: femoral nerve (high articular branches), obturator nerve, accessory obturator nerve when present. The anterior capsule has most of the sensory supply.
Posterior capsule: nerve to quadratus femoris (the main one), with branches from the sciatic and superior gluteal nerves.
PENG: local anaesthetic under the psoas tendon on bone between the AIIS and the iliopubic eminence, where the femoral and accessory obturator articular branches cross.
Motor sparing: it targets articular branches, not the femoral nerve trunk. At 20 ml the quadriceps is often spared, not reliably (in one trial about half had some weakness at 3 hours). Larger volumes or a superficial injection reach the femoral nerve.
Limits: no skin cover (add LFCN), posterior capsule not covered, obturator branches inconsistently.

PRACTICE QUESTION

An 82-year-old is listed for a cemented hemiarthroplasty through an anterolateral approach. Plan the regional analgesia.

Model answer points
Before positioning for spinal: PENG (or supra-inguinal fascia iliaca) 20–30 minutes before, for capsular pain on movement.
PENG 20 ml of 0.2% ropivacaine plus LFCN 5 ml of 0.2%: total 50 mg, within the maximum for a frail 50 kg patient.
The LFCN covers the lateral thigh incision; the PENG covers the anterior capsule; quadriceps spared for early walking.
Multimodal: regular paracetamol, opioid rescue; avoid or use NSAIDs with great caution in frail older patients.
Watch for bone cement implantation syndrome; communicate before cementing.

Supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block

A volume block of the plane under fascia iliaca, injected above the inguinal ligament so the local anaesthetic runs cranially into the iliac fossa over iliacus. It reliably blocks the femoral nerve and the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (LFCN); the obturator nerve is not reliably blocked.

Position

Supine, leg straight. Expose the groin from above the ASIS to the upper thigh. In a patient with a pannus, tape it cranially or have an assistant retract it.

Equipment
Linear probe (curvilinear if deep)
80–100 mm echogenic needle
40 ml of 0.2% ropivacaine in 20 ml syringes, with an extension
Colour Doppler; monitoring and the toxicity kit
Landmarks and scanning

Parasagittal on the ASIS: a bright bony step with a dense shadow; sartorius runs caudally from it, the abdominal wall muscles attach cranially. Slide medially along the inguinal ligament: the ilium drops deeper and the AIIS appears as a hump with iliacus on it. Now find the bow-tie: internal oblique (cranial) and sartorius (caudal) taper towards each other where they meet at the inguinal ligament.

Under the bow-tie, the bright fascia iliaca runs cranially on iliacus, down into the iliac fossa. Colour Doppler: the deep circumflex iliac artery (DCIA) pulses just superficial to fascia iliaca, cranial to the AIIS. Your target is the plane under the fascia, deep to that artery.

Needle approach

In-plane, caudal to cranial, entering 2–4 cm below the inguinal ligament. Pass through sartorius. Fascia iliaca tents, then gives: puncture it cranial to the hump of the AIIS, then hydrodissect and advance a little into the opening plane.

Resistance helps: stiff injection while the fascia is still tented means you are not through yet. Advance until it gives; don’t push harder.

Sonoanatomy

Labels for the exam: internal oblique, sartorius (the bow-tie), fascia iliaca, iliacus, ilium/AIIS, deep circumflex iliac artery. Trace fascia iliaca from caudal to cranial and show where the needle ends: just deep to it, cranial to the AIIS.

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Subcutaneous fat
Iliacus
Target and deposition

Fluid lifts fascia iliaca off iliacus and runs cranially under the DCIA into the iliac fossa (it “unzips” the plane). That cranial spread is what reaches the LFCN and the femoral nerve as they cross iliacus. Wrong planes: fluid pooling above fascia iliaca (deep to internal oblique; a common cause of failure) or a swelling within iliacus.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

40 ml of 0.2% ropivacaine (80 mg)

A volume block: give it all, in 5 ml aliquots with aspiration, watching each one layer out under the fascia. Ease off the probe as you inject. 80 mg is within the usual maximum for an adult. A common teaching maximum for a single dose of ropivacaine is about 3 mg/kg, lower in frail older patients; use lean (ideal) body weight in the light and frail, and count every other dose given that day (an emergency department block, the surgeon’s infiltration).

Local anaesthetic toxicity: Keep the total dose within the maximum for the patient’s weight, especially with bilateral blocks or when combining blocks.

Covers: Femoral nerve and LFCN: anterior and lateral thigh, anterior hip, femur and anterior knee, a strip of medial leg (saphenous). Obturator: sometimes, not reliable.

MECHANISM

The femoral nerve and LFCN both run on iliacus, under fascia iliaca, in the iliac fossa. A large volume injected above the inguinal ligament spreads cranially within that compartment and bathes both. The obturator nerve leaves the medial border of psoas and runs in the pelvis, outside the compartment, so it is reached only when the fluid spreads far medially around psoas.

The fascia iliaca compartment: in front, the back of fascia iliaca; behind, iliacus and psoas; medially, the vertebral column and the origin of psoas; laterally, the inner lip of the iliac crest.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

The LFCN (lateral thigh) is a reliable early test of success. Then the femoral territory (anterior thigh, quadriceps). In a volunteer study with 40 ml, the supra-inguinal approach numbed the medial, anterior and lateral thigh together in 80%, against 30% for the infra-inguinal approach. Allow 20–30 minutes; test the lateral, anterior and medial thigh separately: a missing area tells you which nerve the fluid did not reach.

WHAT IT MISSES
Obturator nerve: not reliably blocked (medial thigh, part of the hip and knee).
Posterior hip and the buttock (sacral plexus, cluneal nerves).
Quadriceps strength: it is lost. This is not a motor-sparing block.
Complications and how to avoid them
Quadriceps weakness: expected. Falls risk; tell the patient and the ward.
Vascular puncture: the DCIA lies on the needle path just above the target. Colour Doppler first.
Peritoneal puncture and bowel injury if the needle goes too deep or too cranial in the iliac fossa. Keep the tip in view.
Local anaesthetic toxicity: large volume; aspirate, aliquots, count the total.
Failure: fluid above fascia iliaca, or intramuscular.
Practical pearls
Find the bow-tie: internal oblique cranial, sartorius caudal.
Colour Doppler: the DCIA marks the plane. Go under it, not into it.
Puncture the fascia cranial to the AIIS hump, then hydrodissect.
Fascia must lift off iliacus. Pooling above it = failed block.
The lateral thigh (LFCN) is your reliable early test.
“Fascia iliaca” is not motor sparing: the quadriceps will be weak.
Obturator nerve: don’t promise it.
Infra-inguinal fascia iliaca: the comparison

The original fascia iliaca block was a landmark technique below the inguinal ligament, now usually done with ultrasound in the femoral view, more lateral than a femoral block, with a larger volume of dilute local anaesthetic, hoping it spreads to the LFCN (and the obturator). See it in the femoral scan viewer, “Infra-inguinal fascia iliaca”.

Landmark: draw the inguinal ligament (ASIS to pubic tubercle) and divide it in thirds. Enter 1 cm below the junction of the lateral and middle thirds with a blunt needle perpendicular to the skin: two pops (fascia lata, then fascia iliaca), then 30–40 ml of a dilute solution with firm pressure distal to the needle.
Ultrasound: transverse at the inguinal crease; under sartorius, lateral to the nerve; tip just under fascia iliaca; watch it spread medially to the nerve and laterally.
From here the fluid spreads more caudally; cranial spread to the LFCN is less consistent and to the obturator rare. In volunteers, MRI showed spread to the obturator nerve’s location in 1 of 10 infra-inguinal blocks against 8 of 10 supra-inguinal ones (that is spread, not a reliable clinical block).
An older placebo-controlled trial found no benefit from an infra-inguinal fascia iliaca block after total hip arthroplasty. That result does not apply to the supra-inguinal approach, which reduced morphine use against no block in a later trial.
It remains useful: quick, far from the nerve, and taught to emergency staff for hip fracture analgesia.

Catheters

A catheter can be threaded 3–5 cm cranially under fascia iliaca from the supra-inguinal view (Tuohy, in-plane caudal to cranial, hydrodissect, thread, test with fluid while scanning). Used for femoral shaft fractures awaiting surgery or prolonged analgesia; the cost is a weak quadriceps for as long as it runs. Fix it well: the groin is mobile and sweaty.

Consultant corner
When to choose it over PENG: femoral shaft or subtrochanteric fractures, fixation with a nail or screw (lateral thigh and femur), when you want the skin numb for the incision, or in the emergency department where one block must do everything.
After induction: it is a plane block far from the nerve, so it can be done under general anaesthesia (for example after a failed spinal or for an unexpected fixation).
The pannus and the deep fossa: curvilinear probe, longer needle, an assistant; keep the tip in view because peritoneum is not far medially.
Distorted anatomy after hip arthroscopy (fluid extravasation) or previous surgery: rescan from the ASIS each time.
Anticoagulated or on antiplatelets (common in hip fracture): current ASRA and European (ESAIC/ESRA) guidance sets neuraxial-type rules for deep, non-compressible blocks and a risk-benefit judgement for superficial, compressible ones. The infra-inguinal fascia iliaca and femoral blocks are superficial and compressible; the supra-inguinal approach reaches the non-compressible iliac fossa near the DCIA, so weigh it more carefully. A lumbar plexus block follows neuraxial rules.
Explaining the weakness: the patient will not be able to straight-leg raise. Document it, tell physiotherapy, and plan walking for when it wears off.
Frontier: what’s new
PENG or supra-inguinal fascia iliaca for hip fracture? A 2025 randomised trial found the same fall in dynamic pain 30 minutes after either block (20 ml PENG versus 30 ml fascia iliaca). The choice is about motor function and what else you want covered, not about analgesia.
Delirium and outcomes. Nerve blocks for hip fracture reduce pain on movement within 30 minutes, and reduce delirium (high-certainty evidence) and probably chest infection, compared with no block.
Pre-hospital blocks. Paramedic-delivered fascia iliaca blocks are being used and studied in several countries.
Mechanism of plane blocks: spread on the screen correlates imperfectly with sensory loss; what matters is the mass of local anaesthetic that reaches the nerves. Deposit in the right compartment, give the full volume, then test.
Naming. The 2024 ASRA-ESRA consensus agreed to name limb blocks by the target nerve and the anatomical location.
Exam corner

MMED OSCE 2020

Perform a supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block on the model. Trace fascia iliaca on the screen and show where your needle tip will end.

Model answer points
Supine; linear probe; 80–100 mm echogenic needle; 40 ml of 0.2% ropivacaine.
Probe parasagittal on the ASIS, slide medially to the AIIS; find the bow-tie (internal oblique cranial, sartorius caudal).
Trace fascia iliaca as the bright line on iliacus from caudal to cranial, into the iliac fossa; identify the DCIA with colour Doppler just above it.
In-plane, caudal to cranial, through sartorius; puncture fascia iliaca cranial to the AIIS.
Tip ends just deep to fascia iliaca, deep to the DCIA; fluid lifts the fascia off iliacus and spreads cranially.
Aliquots with aspiration; watch for fluid above the fascia or in the muscle.

MMED OSCE 2024

Which nerves does a supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block cover? What sensory and motor effects do you expect?

Model answer points
Femoral nerve: anterior thigh (anterior cutaneous branches), medial leg and ankle (saphenous), the hip and knee joints anteriorly and medially, the femur.
LFCN: lateral thigh. Usually the first area to go numb.
Obturator nerve: sometimes, not reliable.
Motor: quadriceps weakness (knee extension); falls risk.
Doesn’t cover the posterior hip and buttock (sacral plexus).

PRACTICE QUESTION

What are the boundaries of the fascia iliaca compartment, and why does the supra-inguinal approach spread better than the infra-inguinal approach?

Model answer points
Anterior: the posterior surface of fascia iliaca. Posterior: iliacus and psoas. Medial: the vertebral column and the origin of psoas. Lateral: the inner lip of the iliac crest.
The femoral nerve and LFCN run on iliacus in this compartment; the obturator nerve runs medial to psoas, outside it.
Supra-inguinal injection goes straight into the iliac fossa and spreads cranially towards the lumbar plexus; infra-inguinal injection relies on spread back up under the inguinal ligament and tends to go caudally.

Position

Supine, bed flat, hip extended with the leg slightly abducted. Expose the inguinal crease; tape a pannus up and away so the probe can reach the level above the profunda.

Equipment
High-frequency linear probe (the nerve is 2–4 cm deep in most adults)
80 mm echogenic needle (50 mm in a slim patient); nerve stimulator optional
15 ml of 0.4% ropivacaine
Monitoring and the toxicity kit
Landmarks and scanning

Probe transverse on the inguinal crease, parallel to it, over the femoral pulse. Find the femoral artery. If you see two arteries, you are below the origin of the profunda femoris: slide cranially until there is one. The nerve is undivided and easiest to see there.

The nerve is lateral to the artery, on iliopsoas, deep to fascia iliaca: a flattened hyperechoic oval or triangle. Follow it up and down to make sure it is not a lymph node, and to see where it divides.

Needle approach

In-plane, lateral to medial. The nerve is the most lateral structure in the neurovascular bundle, so the needle reaches it without crossing a vessel. A first give at fascia lata, then fascia iliaca tents and gives. Puncture fascia iliaca lateral to the nerve and stop at its lateral corner.

Sonoanatomy

The five structures to name (an international consensus on basic blocks): femoral artery, femoral vein, iliopsoas, fascia lata and fascia iliaca, with the femoral nerve as the target. Add sartorius laterally and pectineus medially. The femoral sheath holds the artery and vein; the nerve is outside the sheath, behind fascia iliaca.

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Subcutaneous fat
Iliopsoas
Target and deposition

Fluid under fascia iliaca, lifting it and spreading around the nerve, ideally a doughnut, though a pool against the deep or superficial surface of the nerve is enough. Correct injection pushes the nerve away from the needle. Fluid spreading above fascia iliaca (between it and fascia lata) cannot reach the nerve.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

15 ml of 0.4% ropivacaine (60 mg)

In 5 ml aliquots, aspirating between. Never inject against high resistance: the tip may be in the nerve or still on the fascia.

Local anaesthetic toxicity: Keep the total dose within the maximum for the patient’s weight, especially with bilateral blocks or when combining blocks.

Covers: Anterior and medial thigh to the knee, the femur, the anterior knee, and a strip of medial leg to the medial malleolus (saphenous).

MECHANISM

The femoral nerve (L2–L4, posterior divisions) leaves the lateral border of psoas, runs in the groove between psoas and iliacus under fascia iliaca, and enters the thigh behind the inguinal ligament, lateral to the artery. It divides within a few centimetres: an anterior division (sartorius, pectineus, medial and intermediate cutaneous nerves of the thigh) and a posterior division (quadriceps, the saphenous nerve, articular branches to the hip and knee).

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Dense skin and bone cover of the anterior thigh. For hip fracture it helps: the femoral nerve supplies part of the anterior capsule and much of the femur. The quadriceps is weak: in volunteers, a femoral nerve block cut quadriceps strength to about a tenth of baseline and worsened balance, while an adductor canal block left both near baseline.

WHAT IT MISSES
LFCN (lateral thigh): a “3-in-1” block, despite the name, rarely reaches the obturator and only sometimes the LFCN.
Obturator (medial thigh, part of the hip and knee).
Sciatic (posterior thigh, posterior knee, the leg below the knee except the saphenous strip).
Complications and how to avoid them
Falls from quadriceps weakness: the patient must not walk unaided until it has worn off. Tell the ward.
Vascular puncture and intravascular injection: the artery is right beside the nerve; the vein occasionally lies partly deep to the artery, and rarely the anatomy is variant, so scan with Doppler first. Ease off the probe, Doppler, aspirate.
Nerve injury: rare. Avoid needle–nerve contact; stop with high pressure or pain.
Infection with catheters in the groin.
Practical pearls
One artery, not two: block above the profunda.
Nerve lateral, under fascia iliaca. Vessels in the sheath; nerve outside it.
Two gives: fascia lata, then fascia iliaca.
Don’t chase a full doughnut: a pool on one side is enough.
Twitch you want: “dancing patella” (quadriceps). Sartorius alone is not enough.
A femoral block means a weak leg: falls precautions are part of the block.
Nerve stimulator endpoints

Ultrasound is the main guide; a stimulator confirms the nerve. Start at about 1 mA (0.1 ms, 2 Hz) and aim for the right twitch at 0.3–0.5 mA. A twitch that persists below 0.2 mA suggests the tip is in or against the nerve: withdraw a little before injecting.

Quadriceps twitch with the patella moving up (“dancing patella”): posterior division. The right endpoint.
Sartorius twitch (a band across the medial thigh, no patellar movement): anterior division, or a direct muscle twitch. Redirect slightly lateral and deeper.
Iliopsoas twitch (hip flexion): too deep. Withdraw.
No twitch at high current with ultrasound showing good spread: trust the spread.
Landmark technique

Supine. Draw the inguinal ligament (ASIS to pubic tubercle), feel the femoral pulse at or just below it, and insert the needle 1–2 cm lateral to the pulse, at the crease. With a stimulator, advance until the quadriceps twitch appears. Two pops (fascia lata, fascia iliaca) may be felt with a short-bevel needle. Ultrasound has largely replaced this: it shows the vein’s position, the fascia and the spread.

Catheters

Five steps: needle placement, injection through the needle to confirm the plane, catheter advancement (2–4 cm past the tip), injection through the catheter while scanning, and securing it. A more lateral entry leaves more catheter in iliacus, which holds it better than fat. A common regimen is 0.2% ropivacaine at about 5 ml/h with patient-controlled boluses, as your pain service directs. The quadriceps stays weak while it runs.

Consultant corner
Femoral or fascia iliaca for a hip fracture? The 2020 Association of Anaesthetists guideline accepts either; the fascia iliaca block may give better incisional cover (it adds the LFCN). For femoral shaft fractures a femoral block works well and quickly.
Above-knee amputation in a sick patient (pure regional): femoral, sciatic (subgluteal or transgluteal, which also catches the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve), LFCN and obturator. A supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block can replace the femoral and LFCN injections. See the amputation planner, the sciatic block and the obturator block.
The femoral-to-adductor continuum: the further distal along the femoral triangle and adductor canal, the more selectively sensory (saphenous) the block, at the cost of losing the hip and upper thigh. See the femoral triangle and adductor canal block.
Anticoagulated? The femoral nerve block is superficial and compressible, so it is often the safer choice when a drug is still active; it is a risk-benefit judgement under the ASRA and European guidance, not a neuraxial rule.
Difficult views after hip arthroscopy (fluid pushes everything deeper) or with lymph nodes: scan from the artery outwards; a nerve can be traced, a node cannot.
Anisotropy: tilt the probe cranially or caudally; the nerve often brightens after the first 1–2 ml.
Frontier: what’s new
Motor-sparing alternatives have displaced the femoral nerve block for elective hip and knee surgery: PENG (hip), adductor canal and femoral triangle blocks (knee). The PROSPECT guideline for total hip arthroplasty does not recommend a femoral nerve block, as its adverse effects (weakness, falls) outweigh the benefits there.
Hip fracture PENG versus femoral: in a randomised trial, PENG gave less pain in recovery than a femoral nerve block (no difference by the next day) and better quadriceps strength, in recovery and still on day 1.
Opening injection pressure: high opening pressure goes with needle–nerve or needle–fascia contact during femoral block. Pressure monitoring (or a syringe you can feel) adds a safety signal.
Naming: “3-in-1 block” is obsolete. Call it a femoral nerve block, or a fascia iliaca block if you are targeting the compartment.
Exam corner

MMED OSCE 2020

AKA: femoral (anterior thigh, femur), LFCN (lateral thigh), obturator (medial thigh), sciatic (posterior thigh and femur) and the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve (posterior thigh skin), so a transgluteal or subgluteal sciatic block is preferred.
Neuraxial anaesthesia is often simpler; pure peripheral blocks suit the patient too sick for it. (Sciatic and obturator blocks: see the thigh and knee pages.)

PRACTICE QUESTION

Describe the boundaries and contents of the femoral triangle.

Model answer points
Superior: inguinal ligament. Lateral: medial border of sartorius. Medial: medial border of adductor longus.
Roof: fascia lata (with the cribriform fascia over the saphenous opening), subcutaneous tissue, skin.
Floor: iliopsoas, pectineus and adductor longus.
Contents, lateral to medial: femoral nerve (outside the sheath, deep to fascia iliaca), femoral artery, femoral vein, femoral canal (lymphatics, the node of Cloquet). The sheath holds artery, vein and canal.
The apex leads into the adductor canal.

Probe transverse, 1–2 cm below and medial to the ASIS, parallel to the inguinal ligament. Identify sartorius (medial) and tensor fasciae latae (lateral). Between them, fascia lata splits into a flat, fat-filled tunnel; the LFCN is a small hypoechoic oval in it. Use the lateral edge of sartorius as your anchor rather than hunting for the nerve.

Trace it: cranially the nerve moves medially over sartorius towards the inguinal ligament; caudally the gap widens and the nerve drifts laterally and may divide. If you start in the femoral view, slide laterally following sartorius.

Needle approach

In-plane, lateral to medial, at a shallow angle, staying above TFL. Fascia lata tents and gives; stop in the tunnel just lateral to the nerve. Out-of-plane from caudal also suits this tiny, shallow target: walk the tip down, then hydrodissect.

Superficial to deep: skin, subcutaneous fat, fascia lata (splitting into the tunnel), sartorius medially and TFL laterally, rectus femoris deeper. The nerve is only a few square millimetres in cross-section (larger in meralgia): use the highest frequency.

Rectus femoris
Target and deposition

Covers: The lateral thigh, from below the greater trochanter towards the knee; the area varies a lot between people.

MECHANISM

The LFCN (L2–L3) leaves the lateral border of psoas, crosses iliacus under fascia iliaca towards the ASIS, and passes under (sometimes through) the inguinal ligament, usually within about 2 cm medial to the ASIS. It enters the thigh in the fascia lata tunnel between sartorius and TFL and divides into anterior and posterior branches. Purely sensory.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

In volunteers, a 10 ml tunnel injection numbed the lateral thigh in 95% but reached the proximal branches in only about two thirds; the numb area usually started several centimetres below the greater trochanter. Expect no better from the 5 ml dose. So for a hip incision near the trochanter, check the top of the incision line and plan infiltration.

WHAT IT MISSES
The hip joint (add PENG or fascia iliaca).
The upper end of a lateral incision over the trochanter, often (subcostal and iliohypogastric branches there).
A posterior incision (buttock skin: cluneal nerves).
Complications and how to avoid them
Few. Nerve injury (tiny nerve, shallow: don’t needle it), bruising, intramuscular injection into TFL (failure). It is purely sensory: no weakness, so it is safe for early walking.
Practical pearls
Sartorius medial, TFL lateral, a fat-filled tunnel between: the nerve lives there.
Target the tunnel, not the nerve.
Shallow: 0.5–1 cm. Shallow angle, shallow depth.
No twitch: it is sensory. Tingling down the lateral thigh confirms it.
PENG + LFCN = joint + incision, quadriceps spared.
The numb patch varies: test the top of the incision before relying on it.
Consultant corner
Variable anatomy: the nerve may lie up to several centimetres medial to the ASIS, pass over the ASIS, pierce the inguinal ligament, or already be divided at block level. If no single oval appears, scan medially and laterally, or inject in the tunnel or under the ligament.
Meralgia paraesthetica (entrapment where the nerve passes under the inguinal ligament near the ASIS): a diagnostic block with local anaesthetic (± steroid) relieves the burning lateral thigh pain; hydrodissection and, for refractory cases, pulsed radiofrequency are used. Nerves in meralgia lie closer to the ASIS and are larger in cross-section on ultrasound.
On its own after total hip arthroplasty an LFCN block helps only some patients: in a placebo-controlled trial it reduced pain on movement, but about four in ten did not respond, and coverage of posterior and lateral incision lines was limited in volunteers.
Lithotomy and prone positioning can compress the LFCN: a postoperative numb lateral thigh is not always the block.
Frontier: what’s new
The fat-filled flat tunnel technique (injecting the fascia lata duplication between sartorius and TFL, tracking the tip) improved reach to the proximal branches. Volume and site for proximal (trochanteric) coverage are still being worked out.
PENG plus LFCN is now a standard motor-sparing combination for hip arthroplasty; a recent meta-analysis showed better quadriceps strength and earlier walking than fascia iliaca blocks, with similar or slightly lower pain scores.
Ultrasound diagnosis of meralgia: a larger nerve cross-section at the inguinal ligament supports the diagnosis.
Exam corner

PRACTICE QUESTION

A patient will have a total hip arthroplasty through a lateral incision with a PENG block. What does the PENG miss, and how would you cover it?

Model answer points
PENG covers the anterior capsule (femoral and accessory obturator articular branches), not the skin.
Lateral incision: LFCN territory (L2–L3), plus the iliohypogastric and subcostal branches over the upper end near the trochanter.
LFCN block in the fat-filled tunnel between sartorius and TFL, 1–2 cm below and medial to the ASIS: 5 ml of 0.2% ropivacaine.
Check the proximal incision; ask the surgeon for infiltration over the trochanter and the posterior capsule.
Alternative: supra-inguinal fascia iliaca (femoral + LFCN) at the cost of quadriceps weakness.

PRACTICE QUESTION

What is meralgia paraesthetica? Describe the course of the LFCN.

Model answer points
Entrapment neuropathy of the LFCN: burning pain, numbness or tingling of the anterolateral thigh; no weakness, no reflex change.
Risks: obesity, tight belts, pregnancy, diabetes, positioning (prone, lithotomy), surgery near the ASIS.
Course: L2–L3; lateral border of psoas; across iliacus under fascia iliaca; under the inguinal ligament near the ASIS; into the fascia lata tunnel between sartorius and TFL; anterior and posterior branches.

CHAPTER 6 OF 6 · HIP BLOCKS

Hip fracture: the regional pathway

From the emergency department to the ward: when to block, which block for which operation, and how blocks fit with spinal anaesthesia, delirium prevention and early walking.

KEY POINTS

Treat pain immediately on arrival, including in people with dementia. Reassess within 30 minutes.
Offer a nerve block in the emergency department (fascia iliaca or femoral) and again at surgery if at least 6 hours have passed.
A block before positioning for spinal reduces the need for sedation and IV opioid.
Blocks reduce pain on movement, delirium and probably chest infection. They are not a substitute for early surgery (day of or day after admission).
Match the block to the operation: arthroplasty → PENG + LFCN (or fascia iliaca); fixation → fascia iliaca.
Step by step
1

Emergency department

Regular paracetamol, titrated opioid, and a fascia iliaca block (supra- or infra-inguinal) or femoral nerve block by trained staff, ideally with ultrasound. Assess pain on movement, not only at rest; in dementia use an observational pain score. NSAIDs are best avoided in frail older patients.

2

Before theatre

Correct what can be corrected quickly (fluids, electrolytes, anaemia, anticoagulation) without delaying surgery. On an anticoagulant or antiplatelet drug, choose the block by depth and compressibility: femoral and infra-inguinal fascia iliaca are superficial and compressible; the supra-inguinal approach and PENG are deeper and need more thought; spinal and lumbar plexus blocks follow the neuraxial timings (ASRA and European guidance). Check when the first block was given and how much local anaesthetic it used: count it towards the total.

3

Positioning for spinal

Give (or repeat) the block 20–30 minutes before moving the patient. Sitting, or lateral with the fractured side down for a unilateral hyperbaric spinal, both become tolerable. If more is needed, a small titrated dose of a short-acting analgesic is better than heavy sedation.

4

In theatre

Spinal or general anaesthesia (the outcomes are similar; offer a choice), with age-appropriate, lower doses, a nerve block, minimal or no sedation and careful blood pressure control. For a cemented stem, brief the team about cementing.

5

After

Paracetamol, opioid rescue, and a plan for when the block wears off. Mobilise on the day after surgery: a motor-sparing block (PENG + LFCN) helps; after a fascia iliaca or femoral block, check quadriceps strength before standing. Continuous catheters are rarely needed and may slow mobilisation.

Delirium, opioids and outcomes
Nerve blocks versus none (a large systematic review of randomised trials): less pain on movement within 30 minutes (about 2.5 points on a 0–10 scale), less delirium (about 1 case prevented for every 12 patients blocked), probably less chest infection (about 1 in 7) and earlier first mobilisation. No proven effect on death or myocardial infarction, because the trials were too small to show one.
Delirium prophylaxis: in one trial, a fascia iliaca block on admission reduced delirium in patients at intermediate risk, though not in the highest-risk group.
Spinal or general? A large North American trial found no difference in death or inability to walk at 60 days, or in delirium. Choose by the patient; what matters is good technique, low doses, avoiding hypotension, and a block either way.
Opioid sparing matters most in the frail: opioids add to delirium, constipation, nausea and falls.

WARNING

Bone cement implantation syndrome

After cemented hemiarthroplasty, about 1 in 5 patients have some cardiorespiratory upset, about 1 in 50 a severe reaction and about 1 in 200 a cardiac arrest. Identify high-risk patients (frail, poor heart function, pulmonary hypertension), agree roles at the team brief, and watch the blood pressure closely at cementing, with vasopressor ready. The surgeon washes and dries the canal and uses a cement gun with retrograde filling.

NOTE

Guidance in brief

The 2020 Association of Anaesthetists guideline recommends single-shot nerve blocks in the emergency department and at surgery (at least 6 hours apart), femoral or fascia iliaca blocks (the latter possibly better for the incision), ultrasound guidance, and routine use of blocks with spinal or general anaesthesia. It judged pericapsular techniques (including PENG) not yet formally assessed in hip fracture and suggested them for posterior approaches; trials since have compared PENG favourably with fascia iliaca and femoral blocks. NICE advises surgery on the day of or the day after admission, cemented implants for arthroplasty, a sliding hip screw for most trochanteric fractures and a nail for subtrochanteric ones.

Exam corner

PRACTICE QUESTION

An 80-year-old woman is admitted with a fractured neck of femur after a fall. How would you optimise her pain before surgery?

Model answer points
Assess pain on arrival, 30 minutes after analgesia, hourly until settled, then routinely; use an observational tool if cognitively impaired.
Immediate analgesia even with dementia; enough to allow investigations and passive movement.
Regular paracetamol; titrated opioid; a nerve block (fascia iliaca or femoral) by trained staff, ideally ultrasound-guided.
Avoid NSAIDs in the frail older patient.
Repeat the block at surgery if 6 hours or more have passed; count the total local anaesthetic dose.
Do not let the block delay surgery: aim for the day of or after admission.

PRACTICE QUESTION

Compare the PENG block and the supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block for a patient with a hip fracture.

Model answer points
PENG: on bone under the psoas tendon between the AIIS and the IPE; femoral and accessory obturator articular branches; 20 ml; quadriceps usually spared; no skin.
Supra-inguinal fascia iliaca: under fascia iliaca above the inguinal ligament, spreading into the iliac fossa; femoral nerve and LFCN; 40 ml; quadriceps weak; covers the anterior and lateral thigh skin.
Analgesia before surgery: similar in trials.
Choose PENG (+ LFCN) for arthroplasty and early walking; fascia iliaca for fixation, femoral shaft fractures, or one block to do everything.
Neither reliably blocks the obturator nerve or the posterior capsule.

PRACTICE QUESTION

After a cemented hemiarthroplasty under spinal, your patient becomes agitated in recovery and pulls out her cannula. How do you manage her?

Model answer points
Safety first: call for help, protect the patient, ABC, oxygen; check glucose.
Look for causes: hypoxia, hypotension, pain (is the block wearing off?), urinary retention, drugs (opioids, anticholinergics), sepsis, electrolytes, alcohol withdrawal, a new stroke; bone cement implantation syndrome if early.
Use a delirium screen (for example 4AT); treat the cause; non-drug measures first (glasses, hearing aids, family, reorientation).
Small dose of an antipsychotic only if dangerous and other measures fail; avoid benzodiazepines unless withdrawal.
Prevention: good analgesia with blocks, opioid sparing, avoid deep sedation, early mobilisation, orthogeriatric care.

CHAPTER 1 OF 6 · HIP BLOCKS

Anatomy: the lumbar plexus and the hip

Every hip block is a choice of which branch of the lumbar plexus to catch, where. Learn where the nerves cross the groin and which of them supply the joint, and the choice of block follows.

KEY POINTS

The lumbar plexus (L1–L4, with T12) forms inside psoas. The three nerves that matter here: femoral (L2–L4), lateral femoral cutaneous (L2–L3) and obturator (L2–L4).
Femoral and LFCN leave the lateral border of psoas and run on iliacus under fascia iliaca. The obturator leaves the medial border and runs in the pelvis, outside the fascia iliaca compartment.
At the groin the femoral nerve is lateral to the artery and outside the femoral sheath; the LFCN passes under the inguinal ligament near the ASIS.
The anterior hip capsule (most of the joint’s sensory supply) is supplied by the femoral, obturator and accessory obturator nerves; the posterior capsule by the nerve to quadratus femoris, sciatic and superior gluteal branches.
Hip pain is often felt in the knee: the femoral and obturator nerves supply both joints.

Who supplies the hip joint

Hilton’s law: a nerve that supplies a muscle crossing a joint also supplies the joint. So the hip gets branches from the femoral, obturator and sciatic territories, and the pattern varies between people.

Anterior capsule (the main source of pain after fracture and arthroplasty): femoral nerve (high articular branches that leave the nerve above the inguinal ligament; classically also from the nerve to rectus femoris), obturator nerve, and the accessory obturator nerve when present.
Posterior capsule: nerve to quadratus femoris (the main supply), with branches from the sciatic nerve and the superior gluteal nerve (and in some studies the inferior gluteal nerve).

Why PENG works (and what it doesn’t do)

The logic in four lines

The femoral and accessory obturator branches to the anterior capsule cross the bone between the AIIS and the iliopubic eminence, under the psoas tendon.
Local anaesthetic placed on that bone, under the tendon, catches them before they reach the capsule, while the femoral nerve trunk lies more superficially, on iliopsoas under fascia iliaca.
So the joint is numbed and the quadriceps usually works. The skin is not numbed (no cutaneous nerve runs there).
The obturator branches arrive lower and further in, so they are caught inconsistently, and the posterior capsule not at all.

EXAM PEARL

For the viva

“The anterior hip capsule is supplied by the femoral, obturator and accessory obturator nerves; the posterior capsule by the nerve to quadratus femoris, with sciatic and superior gluteal branches. A PENG block puts local anaesthetic under the psoas tendon between the AIIS and the iliopubic eminence, where the femoral and accessory obturator articular branches run, so it treats capsular pain while sparing the quadriceps. It doesn’t cover the skin, so for arthroplasty I add an LFCN block.”

It is a deep block with risks of epidural spread, retroperitoneal haematoma and toxicity; it has largely been replaced by the anterior blocks on this page for hip surgery.

Position

Landmarks and scanning

Transverse on the ASIS, then slide caudally onto the AIIS. Keep the lateral end there and rotate the medial end caudally about 45°, so the probe lies along the superior pubic ramus, roughly parallel to the inguinal crease. Slide or tilt until AIIS, psoas tendon and iliopubic eminence share one view. The femoral artery should sit at the medial edge of the image, superficial: your safety landmark.

Needle approach

In-plane, lateral to medial, entering 1–2 cm lateral to the probe so the shaft clears the AIIS. Through sartorius (or rectus femoris), fascia iliaca and iliopsoas, then under the psoas tendon to bone. Withdraw 1 mm and aspirate.

The skin entry is close to the LFCN: if infiltration or the needle produces a shoot down the lateral thigh, move the entry point.

Covers: The anterior hip capsule (femoral and accessory obturator articular branches; obturator branches inconsistently). No skin: add an LFCN block or infiltration for the incision.

MECHANISM

The anterior capsule carries most of the joint’s sensory supply. In cadavers, high articular branches of the femoral nerve run between the AIIS and the iliopubic eminence, and the accessory obturator nerve, when present, crosses the eminence. Fluid under the psoas tendon sits right there. The obturator nerve’s articular branches reach the capsule further medially and inferiorly (near the inferomedial acetabulum), so a PENG block reaches them inconsistently.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Good for hip joint pain on movement (positioning, flexion). Imaging in patients shows the injectate staying mostly in and around iliopsoas, so think of it mainly as a block of the femoral (and accessory obturator) articular branches. Motor sparing is likely at about 20 ml, not guaranteed: test quadriceps strength before the patient stands.

WHAT IT MISSES
The skin incision (LFCN laterally; subcostal and iliohypogastric branches over the buttock).
The posterior capsule (nerve to quadratus femoris, sciatic, superior gluteal branches): relevant for a posterior approach.
The femoral shaft and lateral thigh: fixation with a sliding hip screw or nail is less well covered than arthroplasty.
Obturator articular branches: often.
Complications and how to avoid them
Quadriceps weakness from spread to the femoral nerve (volume, or a superficial or intramuscular injection). Warn the patient and the ward: falls risk.
Vascular puncture: femoral artery and vein medially; small vessels near the pubic ramus (for example pubic branches) along the path. Colour Doppler, aspirate, aliquots.
LFCN injury at the skin entry.
Intra-articular or intraneural injection: rare; stop with high pressure or pain.
Local anaesthetic toxicity, especially when adding other blocks.
Practical pearls
Bone, tendon, bone: AIIS laterally, eminence medially, tendon in the groove between.
The tendon must lift off bone. A swelling in the muscle is the wrong plane.
PENG is for the joint, not the skin: add the LFCN for an anterior or lateral incision.
Femoral artery at the medial edge of the screen: you are not going there.
Stiff to inject on bone? The tip may be in periosteum, tendon or capsule (iliofemoral ligament): back 1 mm or turn the bevel.
Test quadriceps before the first walk. Motor sparing is likely, not certain.
Consultant corner
Arthroplasty versus fixation. PENG suits capsular pain: displaced intracapsular fractures, hemiarthroplasty and total hip arthroplasty.
Screw or nail? The pain is the lateral thigh and the femur below the capsule: a supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block (femoral plus LFCN) usually fits better. Before surgery, PENG often still helps an intertrochanteric fracture.
Which incision? Anterior and anterolateral approaches: PENG plus LFCN covers most of it. A posterior approach crosses the buttock (not LFCN territory) and the posterior capsule: add surgical infiltration.
PENG versus supra-inguinal fascia iliaca. In trials the two give similar pain relief (hip fracture before surgery; total hip arthroplasty after it). PENG preserves quadriceps and hip adductor strength better. Choose PENG when early walking matters; choose fascia iliaca when you also want the anterior and lateral thigh numb, or for femoral fractures.
The hard patient. Obese: curvilinear probe, a steeper approach, an assistant to retract the pannus. After previous hip surgery or with heterotopic bone, the bony landmarks still guide you; the tendon may be hard to see.
Volume and the quadriceps. At 20 ml, motor sparing is common, not reliable: in one hip arthroplasty trial about half had some quadriceps weakness at 3 hours and a quarter at 6 hours. Test the quadriceps before standing; don’t exceed the department’s 20 ml.
The cadaver numbers. Dye reached the femoral nerve trunk in half the specimens at 20 ml and in all at 30 ml; the femoral-sparing volume (90% of cases) was about 13 ml.
Anticoagulated or on antiplatelets? PENG is deep, on bone, and not easily compressed. Current ASRA and European (ESAIC/ESRA) guidance treats deep, non-compressible blocks more like neuraxial ones; weigh the benefit (often a single-shot PENG or fascia iliaca is still worth it) against the bleeding risk, and prefer a superficial, compressible block when the drug is fully active.
Catheters under the psoas tendon have been described; they are not standard.
Frontier: what’s new
How does it really work? CT imaging in patients shows PENG injectate staying mostly within the fascia of iliacus and psoas, with little capsular spread and none into the obturator foramen. Cadaver work agrees that the obturator articular branches are rarely reached. The analgesia is probably from the femoral nerve’s articular branches inside iliopsoas: it is a ‘femoral articular’ block more than a true pericapsular one.
PENG plus LFCN versus fascia iliaca. A recent meta-analysis of six hip surgery trials favoured the combination for quadriceps strength and earlier walking, with slightly lower resting pain and no clear difference in opioid use.
PENG versus local infiltration after total hip arthroplasty: similar pain and opioid use in pooled trials. The PROSPECT guideline for total hip arthroplasty recommends fascia iliaca block or local infiltration analgesia (with paracetamol, an NSAID and IV dexamethasone); PENG had too little evidence when it was written.
Chronic hip pain. The same articular branches (between the AIIS and eminence, and at the inferomedial acetabulum) are targets for radiofrequency ablation and cryoneurolysis in patients unfit for arthroplasty.
Exam corner

PRACTICE QUESTION

Describe the sensory innervation of the hip joint. Which part does a PENG block target, and why is it described as motor sparing?

Model answer points
Hilton’s law: the nerves supplying the muscles that cross the hip also supply the joint.
Anterior capsule: femoral nerve (high articular branches), obturator nerve, accessory obturator nerve when present. The anterior capsule has most of the sensory supply.
Posterior capsule: nerve to quadratus femoris (the main one), with branches from the sciatic and superior gluteal nerves.
PENG: local anaesthetic under the psoas tendon on bone between the AIIS and the iliopubic eminence, where the femoral and accessory obturator articular branches cross.
Motor sparing: it targets articular branches, not the femoral nerve trunk. At 20 ml the quadriceps is often spared, not reliably (in one trial about half had some weakness at 3 hours). Larger volumes or a superficial injection reach the femoral nerve.
Limits: no skin cover (add LFCN), posterior capsule not covered, obturator branches inconsistently.

PRACTICE QUESTION

An 82-year-old is listed for a cemented hemiarthroplasty through an anterolateral approach. Plan the regional analgesia.

Model answer points
Before positioning for spinal: PENG (or supra-inguinal fascia iliaca) 20–30 minutes before, for capsular pain on movement.
PENG 20 ml of 0.2% ropivacaine plus LFCN 5 ml of 0.2%: total 50 mg, within the maximum for a frail 50 kg patient.
The LFCN covers the lateral thigh incision; the PENG covers the anterior capsule; quadriceps spared for early walking.
Multimodal: regular paracetamol, opioid rescue; avoid or use NSAIDs with great caution in frail older patients.
Watch for bone cement implantation syndrome; communicate before cementing.

Position

Supine, leg straight. Expose the groin from above the ASIS to the upper thigh. In a patient with a pannus, tape it cranially or have an assistant retract it.

Equipment
Linear probe (curvilinear if deep)
80–100 mm echogenic needle
40 ml of 0.2% ropivacaine in 20 ml syringes, with an extension
Colour Doppler; monitoring and the toxicity kit
Landmarks and scanning

Parasagittal on the ASIS: a bright bony step with a dense shadow; sartorius runs caudally from it, the abdominal wall muscles attach cranially. Slide medially along the inguinal ligament: the ilium drops deeper and the AIIS appears as a hump with iliacus on it. Now find the bow-tie: internal oblique (cranial) and sartorius (caudal) taper towards each other where they meet at the inguinal ligament.

Under the bow-tie, the bright fascia iliaca runs cranially on iliacus, down into the iliac fossa. Colour Doppler: the deep circumflex iliac artery (DCIA) pulses just superficial to fascia iliaca, cranial to the AIIS. Your target is the plane under the fascia, deep to that artery.

Needle approach

In-plane, caudal to cranial, entering 2–4 cm below the inguinal ligament. Pass through sartorius. Fascia iliaca tents, then gives: puncture it cranial to the hump of the AIIS, then hydrodissect and advance a little into the opening plane.

Resistance helps: stiff injection while the fascia is still tented means you are not through yet. Advance until it gives; don’t push harder.

Sonoanatomy

Labels for the exam: internal oblique, sartorius (the bow-tie), fascia iliaca, iliacus, ilium/AIIS, deep circumflex iliac artery. Trace fascia iliaca from caudal to cranial and show where the needle ends: just deep to it, cranial to the AIIS.

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Subcutaneous fat
Iliacus
Target and deposition

Fluid lifts fascia iliaca off iliacus and runs cranially under the DCIA into the iliac fossa (it “unzips” the plane). That cranial spread is what reaches the LFCN and the femoral nerve as they cross iliacus. Wrong planes: fluid pooling above fascia iliaca (deep to internal oblique; a common cause of failure) or a swelling within iliacus.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

40 ml of 0.2% ropivacaine (80 mg)

A volume block: give it all, in 5 ml aliquots with aspiration, watching each one layer out under the fascia. Ease off the probe as you inject. 80 mg is within the usual maximum for an adult. A common teaching maximum for a single dose of ropivacaine is about 3 mg/kg, lower in frail older patients; use lean (ideal) body weight in the light and frail, and count every other dose given that day (an emergency department block, the surgeon’s infiltration).

Local anaesthetic toxicity: Keep the total dose within the maximum for the patient’s weight, especially with bilateral blocks or when combining blocks.

The right lower limb. Areas are schematic: nerve territories vary and overlap.
Lateral femoral cutaneous (L2–L3): the outer (lateral) thigh, from just below the anterior superior iliac spine to above the knee
Anterior cutaneous branches of the femoral nerve (intermediate and medial femoral cutaneous, L2–L3): the front and inner side of the thigh, down to the knee
Hip joint, anterior capsule: deep: articular branches of the femoral, obturator and (when present) accessory obturator nerves
Femur: deep: femoral, sciatic and obturator branches (varies along the bone)
Saphenous (L3–L4): the skin below and inside the kneecap, the inner side of the leg, the medial malleolus and the inner side of the foot
Knee joint, anterior and anteromedial capsule: deep: femoral branches (nerves to the vasti, saphenous), the common peroneal laterally and the obturator medially (variable)
Obturator, cutaneous branch (L2–L4): a variable patch of the lower inner thigh; small or absent in many people

Covers: Femoral nerve and LFCN: anterior and lateral thigh, anterior hip, femur and anterior knee, a strip of medial leg (saphenous). Obturator: sometimes, not reliable.

MECHANISM

The femoral nerve and LFCN both run on iliacus, under fascia iliaca, in the iliac fossa. A large volume injected above the inguinal ligament spreads cranially within that compartment and bathes both. The obturator nerve leaves the medial border of psoas and runs in the pelvis, outside the compartment, so it is reached only when the fluid spreads far medially around psoas.

The fascia iliaca compartment: in front, the back of fascia iliaca; behind, iliacus and psoas; medially, the vertebral column and the origin of psoas; laterally, the inner lip of the iliac crest.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

The LFCN (lateral thigh) is a reliable early test of success. Then the femoral territory (anterior thigh, quadriceps). In a volunteer study with 40 ml, the supra-inguinal approach numbed the medial, anterior and lateral thigh together in 80%, against 30% for the infra-inguinal approach. Allow 20–30 minutes; test the lateral, anterior and medial thigh separately: a missing area tells you which nerve the fluid did not reach.

WHAT IT MISSES
Obturator nerve: not reliably blocked (medial thigh, part of the hip and knee).
Posterior hip and the buttock (sacral plexus, cluneal nerves).
Quadriceps strength: it is lost. This is not a motor-sparing block.
Complications and how to avoid them
Quadriceps weakness: expected. Falls risk; tell the patient and the ward.
Vascular puncture: the DCIA lies on the needle path just above the target. Colour Doppler first.
Peritoneal puncture and bowel injury if the needle goes too deep or too cranial in the iliac fossa. Keep the tip in view.
Local anaesthetic toxicity: large volume; aspirate, aliquots, count the total.
Failure: fluid above fascia iliaca, or intramuscular.
Practical pearls
Find the bow-tie: internal oblique cranial, sartorius caudal.
Colour Doppler: the DCIA marks the plane. Go under it, not into it.
Puncture the fascia cranial to the AIIS hump, then hydrodissect.
Fascia must lift off iliacus. Pooling above it = failed block.
The lateral thigh (LFCN) is your reliable early test.
“Fascia iliaca” is not motor sparing: the quadriceps will be weak.
Obturator nerve: don’t promise it.
Infra-inguinal fascia iliaca: the comparison

The original fascia iliaca block was a landmark technique below the inguinal ligament, now usually done with ultrasound in the femoral view, more lateral than a femoral block, with a larger volume of dilute local anaesthetic, hoping it spreads to the LFCN (and the obturator). See it in the femoral scan viewer, “Infra-inguinal fascia iliaca”.

Landmark: draw the inguinal ligament (ASIS to pubic tubercle) and divide it in thirds. Enter 1 cm below the junction of the lateral and middle thirds with a blunt needle perpendicular to the skin: two pops (fascia lata, then fascia iliaca), then 30–40 ml of a dilute solution with firm pressure distal to the needle.
Ultrasound: transverse at the inguinal crease; under sartorius, lateral to the nerve; tip just under fascia iliaca; watch it spread medially to the nerve and laterally.
From here the fluid spreads more caudally; cranial spread to the LFCN is less consistent and to the obturator rare. In volunteers, MRI showed spread to the obturator nerve’s location in 1 of 10 infra-inguinal blocks against 8 of 10 supra-inguinal ones (that is spread, not a reliable clinical block).
An older placebo-controlled trial found no benefit from an infra-inguinal fascia iliaca block after total hip arthroplasty. That result does not apply to the supra-inguinal approach, which reduced morphine use against no block in a later trial.
It remains useful: quick, far from the nerve, and taught to emergency staff for hip fracture analgesia.

Spread	Cranially into the iliac fossa	Mostly caudally and medially
Femoral	Reliable	Reliable
LFCN	Reliable	Variable
Obturator	Sometimes, not reliable	Rare

Catheters

A catheter can be threaded 3–5 cm cranially under fascia iliaca from the supra-inguinal view (Tuohy, in-plane caudal to cranial, hydrodissect, thread, test with fluid while scanning). Used for femoral shaft fractures awaiting surgery or prolonged analgesia; the cost is a weak quadriceps for as long as it runs. Fix it well: the groin is mobile and sweaty.

Consultant corner
When to choose it over PENG: femoral shaft or subtrochanteric fractures, fixation with a nail or screw (lateral thigh and femur), when you want the skin numb for the incision, or in the emergency department where one block must do everything.
After induction: it is a plane block far from the nerve, so it can be done under general anaesthesia (for example after a failed spinal or for an unexpected fixation).
The pannus and the deep fossa: curvilinear probe, longer needle, an assistant; keep the tip in view because peritoneum is not far medially.
Distorted anatomy after hip arthroscopy (fluid extravasation) or previous surgery: rescan from the ASIS each time.
Anticoagulated or on antiplatelets (common in hip fracture): current ASRA and European (ESAIC/ESRA) guidance sets neuraxial-type rules for deep, non-compressible blocks and a risk-benefit judgement for superficial, compressible ones. The infra-inguinal fascia iliaca and femoral blocks are superficial and compressible; the supra-inguinal approach reaches the non-compressible iliac fossa near the DCIA, so weigh it more carefully. A lumbar plexus block follows neuraxial rules.
Explaining the weakness: the patient will not be able to straight-leg raise. Document it, tell physiotherapy, and plan walking for when it wears off.
Frontier: what’s new
PENG or supra-inguinal fascia iliaca for hip fracture? A 2025 randomised trial found the same fall in dynamic pain 30 minutes after either block (20 ml PENG versus 30 ml fascia iliaca). The choice is about motor function and what else you want covered, not about analgesia.
Delirium and outcomes. Nerve blocks for hip fracture reduce pain on movement within 30 minutes, and reduce delirium (high-certainty evidence) and probably chest infection, compared with no block.
Pre-hospital blocks. Paramedic-delivered fascia iliaca blocks are being used and studied in several countries.
Mechanism of plane blocks: spread on the screen correlates imperfectly with sensory loss; what matters is the mass of local anaesthetic that reaches the nerves. Deposit in the right compartment, give the full volume, then test.
Naming. The 2024 ASRA-ESRA consensus agreed to name limb blocks by the target nerve and the anatomical location.
Exam corner

MMED OSCE 2020

Perform a supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block on the model. Trace fascia iliaca on the screen and show where your needle tip will end.

Model answer points
Supine; linear probe; 80–100 mm echogenic needle; 40 ml of 0.2% ropivacaine.
Probe parasagittal on the ASIS, slide medially to the AIIS; find the bow-tie (internal oblique cranial, sartorius caudal).
Trace fascia iliaca as the bright line on iliacus from caudal to cranial, into the iliac fossa; identify the DCIA with colour Doppler just above it.
In-plane, caudal to cranial, through sartorius; puncture fascia iliaca cranial to the AIIS.
Tip ends just deep to fascia iliaca, deep to the DCIA; fluid lifts the fascia off iliacus and spreads cranially.
Aliquots with aspiration; watch for fluid above the fascia or in the muscle.

MMED OSCE 2024

Which nerves does a supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block cover? What sensory and motor effects do you expect?

Model answer points
Femoral nerve: anterior thigh (anterior cutaneous branches), medial leg and ankle (saphenous), the hip and knee joints anteriorly and medially, the femur.
LFCN: lateral thigh. Usually the first area to go numb.
Obturator nerve: sometimes, not reliable.
Motor: quadriceps weakness (knee extension); falls risk.
Doesn’t cover the posterior hip and buttock (sacral plexus).

PRACTICE QUESTION

What are the boundaries of the fascia iliaca compartment, and why does the supra-inguinal approach spread better than the infra-inguinal approach?

Model answer points
Anterior: the posterior surface of fascia iliaca. Posterior: iliacus and psoas. Medial: the vertebral column and the origin of psoas. Lateral: the inner lip of the iliac crest.
The femoral nerve and LFCN run on iliacus in this compartment; the obturator nerve runs medial to psoas, outside it.
Supra-inguinal injection goes straight into the iliac fossa and spreads cranially towards the lumbar plexus; infra-inguinal injection relies on spread back up under the inguinal ligament and tends to go caudally.

CHAPTER 4 OF 6 · HIP AND THIGH · FEMORAL NERVE

Femoral nerve block

Local anaesthetic around the femoral nerve under fascia iliaca, lateral to the femoral artery, at the inguinal crease. It numbs the anterior thigh, the femur, the anterior knee and a strip of medial leg (saphenous), and it weakens the quadriceps.

USE IT FOR

Femoral neck and shaft fractures (also in the emergency department)
Surgery on the femur, patella and quadriceps tendon
Anterior thigh and knee surgery (when quadriceps weakness doesn’t matter)
Part of an above-knee amputation plan (with sciatic, LFCN and obturator)
POSITION

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Dense skin and bone cover of the anterior thigh. For hip fracture it helps: the femoral nerve supplies part of the anterior capsule and much of the femur. The quadriceps is weak: in volunteers, a femoral nerve block cut quadriceps strength to about a tenth of baseline and worsened balance, while an adductor canal block left both near baseline.

WHAT IT MISSES
LFCN (lateral thigh): a “3-in-1” block, despite the name, rarely reaches the obturator and only sometimes the LFCN.
Obturator (medial thigh, part of the hip and knee).
Sciatic (posterior thigh, posterior knee, the leg below the knee except the saphenous strip).
Complications and how to avoid them
Falls from quadriceps weakness: the patient must not walk unaided until it has worn off. Tell the ward.
Vascular puncture and intravascular injection: the artery is right beside the nerve; the vein occasionally lies partly deep to the artery, and rarely the anatomy is variant, so scan with Doppler first. Ease off the probe, Doppler, aspirate.
Nerve injury: rare. Avoid needle–nerve contact; stop with high pressure or pain.
Infection with catheters in the groin.
Practical pearls
One artery, not two: block above the profunda.
Nerve lateral, under fascia iliaca. Vessels in the sheath; nerve outside it.
Two gives: fascia lata, then fascia iliaca.
Don’t chase a full doughnut: a pool on one side is enough.
Twitch you want: “dancing patella” (quadriceps). Sartorius alone is not enough.
A femoral block means a weak leg: falls precautions are part of the block.
Nerve stimulator endpoints

Ultrasound is the main guide; a stimulator confirms the nerve. Start at about 1 mA (0.1 ms, 2 Hz) and aim for the right twitch at 0.3–0.5 mA. A twitch that persists below 0.2 mA suggests the tip is in or against the nerve: withdraw a little before injecting.

Quadriceps twitch with the patella moving up (“dancing patella”): posterior division. The right endpoint.
Sartorius twitch (a band across the medial thigh, no patellar movement): anterior division, or a direct muscle twitch. Redirect slightly lateral and deeper.
Iliopsoas twitch (hip flexion): too deep. Withdraw.
No twitch at high current with ultrasound showing good spread: trust the spread.
Landmark technique

Supine. Draw the inguinal ligament (ASIS to pubic tubercle), feel the femoral pulse at or just below it, and insert the needle 1–2 cm lateral to the pulse, at the crease. With a stimulator, advance until the quadriceps twitch appears. Two pops (fascia lata, fascia iliaca) may be felt with a short-bevel needle. Ultrasound has largely replaced this: it shows the vein’s position, the fascia and the spread.

Catheters

Five steps: needle placement, injection through the needle to confirm the plane, catheter advancement (2–4 cm past the tip), injection through the catheter while scanning, and securing it. A more lateral entry leaves more catheter in iliacus, which holds it better than fat. A common regimen is 0.2% ropivacaine at about 5 ml/h with patient-controlled boluses, as your pain service directs. The quadriceps stays weak while it runs.

Consultant corner
Femoral or fascia iliaca for a hip fracture? The 2020 Association of Anaesthetists guideline accepts either; the fascia iliaca block may give better incisional cover (it adds the LFCN). For femoral shaft fractures a femoral block works well and quickly.
Above-knee amputation in a sick patient (pure regional): femoral, sciatic (subgluteal or transgluteal, which also catches the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve), LFCN and obturator. A supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block can replace the femoral and LFCN injections. See the amputation planner, the sciatic block and the obturator block.
The femoral-to-adductor continuum: the further distal along the femoral triangle and adductor canal, the more selectively sensory (saphenous) the block, at the cost of losing the hip and upper thigh. See the femoral triangle and adductor canal block.
Anticoagulated? The femoral nerve block is superficial and compressible, so it is often the safer choice when a drug is still active; it is a risk-benefit judgement under the ASRA and European guidance, not a neuraxial rule.
Difficult views after hip arthroscopy (fluid pushes everything deeper) or with lymph nodes: scan from the artery outwards; a nerve can be traced, a node cannot.
Anisotropy: tilt the probe cranially or caudally; the nerve often brightens after the first 1–2 ml.
Frontier: what’s new
Motor-sparing alternatives have displaced the femoral nerve block for elective hip and knee surgery: PENG (hip), adductor canal and femoral triangle blocks (knee). The PROSPECT guideline for total hip arthroplasty does not recommend a femoral nerve block, as its adverse effects (weakness, falls) outweigh the benefits there.
Hip fracture PENG versus femoral: in a randomised trial, PENG gave less pain in recovery than a femoral nerve block (no difference by the next day) and better quadriceps strength, in recovery and still on day 1.
Opening injection pressure: high opening pressure goes with needle–nerve or needle–fascia contact during femoral block. Pressure monitoring (or a syringe you can feel) adds a safety signal.
Naming: “3-in-1 block” is obsolete. Call it a femoral nerve block, or a fascia iliaca block if you are targeting the compartment.

Neuraxial anaesthesia is often simpler; pure peripheral blocks suit the patient too sick for it. (Sciatic and obturator blocks: see the thigh and knee pages.)

Lithotomy and prone positioning can compress the LFCN: a postoperative numb lateral thigh is not always the block.

The fat-filled flat tunnel technique (injecting the fascia lata duplication between sartorius and TFL, tracking the tip) improved reach to the proximal branches. Volume and site for proximal (trochanteric) coverage are still being worked out.
